# My Rebuttal as Marcus, the Neighbour

---

## Where I Find Common Ground — and Why That Matters

Let me begin by saying something I did not expect to say: I am genuinely moved by both Claire's reasoning (the primary decision-maker) and Dr. Ellis's framework. Reading their positions carefully, I find that all three of us have converged on the same structural recommendation — Action C, the path of immediate physical separation combined with professional assessment. That convergence is not coincidental. It reflects what a reasonable, evidence-oriented person arrives at when they resist both panic and denial.

But convergence on a headline recommendation does not mean our positions are identical. There are meaningful differences in emphasis, in what each of us sees most clearly, and in what each of us is at risk of missing. I want to engage with those differences honestly — because I think they matter.

---

## My Rebuttal to the Primary Decision-Maker (Claire)

Claire, I respect you. What you've written is thoughtful, loving, and genuinely careful. But I need to name something your framework does not fully address, and it is the thing that keeps me awake at night.

**Your analysis is written entirely from inside the house.**

Your stakeholder table lists Leo, Biscuit, you, your partner, extended family, and a potential adoptive family. My children — who play in your garden — do not appear anywhere in your framework. That is not a criticism of your character; it is an observation about the natural limits of attention when you are in the middle of a crisis. You are focused on the people you can see, the relationships you live inside. I understand that completely.

But here is what I need you to hear: **your decision has consequences that extend beyond your fence line.** If Action C is pursued — which I support — part of what makes it work is that *I know about it*. That the supervision protocols you commit to are communicated to me, so that I can make informed choices about when my children visit, and under what conditions. Your behavioural management plan needs to include a neighbour clause, not out of legal obligation, but out of basic honesty between people who share space and care about each other.

I also want to gently challenge one thing in your framing. You describe the temporary separation option as costing you "a few weeks and some discomfort." I think you may be underestimating the emotional weight of this period — on Leo, on your relationship with David, on yourself. I am not saying this to discourage you; I am saying it because if you underestimate the cost, you may underestimate the support you need. My wife and I are here. Let us actually help, rather than hovering anxiously on our side of the fence wondering what is happening.

**My position remains Action C — but I am updating it to include explicit communication with me as part of the safety protocol.** Not as surveillance. As neighbourliness.

---

## My Rebuttal to Dr. Ellis (External Advisor)

Dr. Ellis, your framework is the most structurally rigorous of the three, and I find very little to dispute in your clinical reasoning. The 8–12 week window, the defined benchmarks, the insistence on veterinary assessment before behavioural judgment — all of this is correct, and I am glad someone with your credentials is saying it clearly.

But I want to raise something your professional framing may inadvertently obscure.

**You describe this situation as a family welfare case. I am living it as a neighbourhood reality.**

Your stakeholder table, like Claire's, does not include me or my children. This is understandable — you were called in by a paediatrician to assess a family, not a street. But the clinical frame can create a kind of boundary around the problem that makes it seem more contained than it is. Biscuit does not stay in the house. He goes into the garden. He occasionally comes through the gate when children are playing. The risk you are carefully managing inside those four walls does not reliably stay there.

I am also mildly concerned about one element of your language. You describe the 8–12 week window as the period within which the family must meet "clear, measurable safety benchmarks." I agree with the principle. But I want to ask: *who monitors compliance with those benchmarks?* You will presumably not be visiting the home every week. Claire and David will be doing their best under significant emotional strain. In my experience as a teacher — someone who has watched students, parents, and institutions commit sincerely to plans they subsequently fail to follow through on — good intentions and good plans diverge in real life more often than professionals expect.

I am not suggesting the family is unreliable. I am suggesting that the plan needs a human accountability structure, not just a clinical one. Someone who can say, gently and without judgment, *"How did this week go? Was the gate locked? Did Biscuit have a bad day?"* That person might be a behaviorist checking in by phone. It might be my wife, who Claire trusts. It might be both.

**I am updating my position to advocate not just for Action C, but for built-in accountability that includes people outside the clinical relationship.** A plan that exists only in a consultant's report and a family's good intentions is more fragile than it needs to be.

---

## One Point Where I Hold Firm

Both Claire and Dr. Ellis frame the decision primarily around **the family's internal experience** — their grief, their guilt, their love, their legal exposure. These things are real and they matter.

But I want to say something that neither of them quite says directly, and that I feel I must say, even if it is uncomfortable.

**I have a right to this information.** Not a legal right — I am aware I have no legal standing here. A *moral* right, as someone whose children are part of the social fabric of this household. The parents' right to make their own decisions about their dog does not extinguish my right to make informed decisions about my children's exposure to that dog. These rights do not conflict — they coexist. But they only coexist if there is honest communication between neighbours.

If the family pursues Action C and never tells me, and my six-year-old wanders through the gate on a Tuesday afternoon during a week when the intervention is going poorly, then the careful ethical reasoning in both of those documents above has failed in its most basic practical function: keeping children safe.

---

## My Revised Final Position

I continue to advocate for **Action C — immediate physical separation, urgent veterinary assessment, certified behavioural intervention, with defined benchmarks and an honest exit plan.** I believe this is the ethically correct path, and I am glad that all three perspectives in this conversation have reached the same conclusion.

**But I am adding one thing that neither of the other frameworks includes:**

> *The intervention plan must include honest, ongoing communication with affected neighbours — specifically, with me — so that I can exercise my own parental judgment about my children's access to the adjoining space.*

This is not a demand. It is an invitation to let me be part of the solution rather than an anxious bystander to it. Claire confided in my wife because she trusts us. I am asking that trust to function in both directions — not just as emotional support, but as practical partnership.

The child's safety is the ceiling. The dog deserves a fair chance. And the neighbours deserve to know.
